items.title: Akiyoshi Toshiko — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: he says that you guys became very, very good friends, very close friends... we developed a lasting friendship

ctx.x: But it‟s okay. Everything works out. But it was, I just … that was a departure for me. And after that, I had a very difficult time, you know, economically at that time. But, I didn‟t stop, so I was somehow … since then, most of the time, I would start playing at a place like a service club, because you could play [jazz], and my best job was in Yokohama, a place called Seamen‟s Club. And it was a small … it was a seamen‟s club. Almost once a week they had a fight, you know, a big fight. The owner, I think, was a…

items.title: Toshiko Akiyoshi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 17, 1999
items.q: some of them noteworthy like Hampton Hawes for example that’s a noted player... there were quite many good players in Japan in the Army and, not Navy, but Air Force band. And they would come and sit in where I had my own group.

ctx.x: No, nothing. So you learn that way. And there’s another very precious lesson in those days, were drafted musicians from here, professional ones, some of them noteworthy like Hampton Hawes for example that’s a noted player. Even those not that noted, Eddie Costa. There was a drum player, later he was playing with Eddie’s group or somebody like that. But anyway, there were quite many good players in Japan in the Army and, not Navy, but Air Force band. And they would come and sit in where I had my own group. And I…
Did you start writing them down, or did they just become memorized immediately yourself?
